technology.seoDescription: Explore the Jalaranu project: from shore facilities and computing modules to heat management, connectivity, and recovery.

hero.h1: Engineering starts with the right questions.
hero.body: Jalaranu explores the underlake datacenter as **one complete system**. Module placement needs to be evaluated together with power, networking, heat management, maintenance, and recovery.

architecture.h2: From shore interfaces to the underwater environment.
body: The project architecture includes four elements: shore-based support facilities, power and communications connections, the computing module, and monitoring and operational management. Their relationships determine how the overall facility can function and recover.
Early visualisations use a truncated square pyramid. This is a design exploration; final geometry, materials, and specifications will follow engineering and test findings.
architecture.visualNote: A block diagram and cross-section showing logical connections, without coordinates or facility-security details.

comparison.h2: Advantages need to be assessed against relevant alternatives.
body: Evaluation should compare the underlake project with land-based solutions using equivalent service requirements, workloads, and assumptions. Relevant comparisons include land-based facilities with conventional cooling and water-based cooling, where applicable to the site under study.

Assessment covers energy, capital expenditure, operating costs, maintenance, connectivity, recovery, environmental effects, and end of life. Potential savings in one component do not in themselves demonstrate a lower total cost.

intro: The underlake project is evaluated against three reference placements at equal service: a terrestrial facility, a hardened bunker, and an undersea deployment. Each trade-off below is an initial assessment to be tested, not a measured result.

A companion ten-year cost model at equal service gives 6.00 million dollars for a terrestrial facility with conventional cooling, 6.34 for a hardened terrestrial facility with lake-water cooling, and 7.85 for the submerged design. Submersion buys capability, not cost saving.
placements.note: Initial framework assessment for discussion. Figures and rankings require measurement and site studies. Screening thermal numbers (a basin-average anomaly of about 0.001 kelvin over fifty years and a twelve-month footprint of 228-509 metres) carry unproven status until measured.

items.title: Terrestrial datacenter
items.body: The mature reference point: established supply chains, easy access, and proven operations. Its costs include energy-intensive cooling, land requirements, and the concentration of strategic data in a few urban corridors. At equal service the ten-year model gives 6.00 million dollars with conventional cooling; the strategic weakness is concentration in a few urban corridors.

items.title: Hardened bunker
items.body: Strong physical protection for critical workloads. The trade-offs are high construction cost, more complex heat rejection, and a facility that is harder to scale than modular surface infrastructure. At 6.34 million dollars with lake-water cooling it is the cheapest hardened comparator in the model, but it carries high construction cost and complex heat rejection.

items.title: Undersea datacenter
items.body: Proven at sea by Project Natick: ocean water removes heat without mechanical cooling. But the maritime threat surface includes submarine cable interception, anchor drag, and contested jurisdiction, with saltwater corrosion and difficult access. Project Natick proved submerged heat rejection at sea; the paper's threat model nonetheless treats the maritime surface (submarine cable interception, anchor drag, contested jurisdiction) as the decisive difference.

items.title: Underlake datacenter
items.body: A lake is not a small ocean. Inland waters sit inside domestic jurisdiction, beyond submarine reach, in quiet freshwater near hydropower and existing communities. Open questions remain: thermal and ecological effects, seismic exposure, acoustic hardening, and retrieval procedures. The model prices the submerged design at 7.85 million dollars: submersion removes direct maritime access paths and keeps the facility in domestic jurisdiction, but thermal, ecological, seismic, acoustic, and retrieval questions remain open and unproven.

body: The project can be evaluated for dedicated computing, storage, or particular infrastructure requirements defined by an organisation. The suitability of each use case must be established through requirements assessment and test evidence.
A use case mentioned here is not a statement that the service is already available or approved to handle sensitive data.

intro: The reference structure breaks the module into 24 numbered components across six systems. The figure is a dimensional engineering draft, not a fabrication drawing.

items.title: Protective enclosure
items.body: Stainless-steel shell, structural stiffeners, and corrosion protection, carried by a ballast skid. Lifting loads pass through four upper padeyes, while the service lid keeps two seals separated by a monitored interspace.

items.title: Computing cassette
items.body: An 8U cassette holds three 2U servers with SSD/NVMe storage and a network switch, under a proposed nitrogen atmosphere with controlled humidity and A/B power and fibre feedthroughs.

items.title: Cooling loop
items.body: A gas-to-liquid coil and fans move heat into a closed coolant circuit through A/B pumps and A/B external heat exchangers. Isolation valves separate branches, and lake water never mixes with internal coolant.

items.title: Power resilience
items.body: An optional LiFePO4 battery UPS sits in a lower bay separated from the computing equipment, targeting a ten-minute reserve at the assumed 2.1 kW load.

items.title: Vibration isolation
items.body: Four captive isolators with cushioned snubbers suspend the server cassette, with flexible connections, electrical bonding, and transport and service locks.

items.title: Monitoring and safety
items.body: Temperature, humidity, oxygen, pressure, and motion sensors, a camera with window and wiper, and a leak-detection tray feed power distribution and safety controls.

inside.note: All stated values are design assumptions, not measurements. Watertightness, operating depth, lifting capacity, and seismic resistance remain to be established through analysis and integrated testing.
